To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) chronic thalamic stimulating electrodes implanted for the treatment of PD-related tremor do not appear to have a significant adverse impact on neuropsychological functioning in most patients, although a minority may experience some decline, (2) the neuropsychological test profile for patients with thalamic electrodes is generally similar to that for patients with PD, and (3) the cognitive effects of chronic stimulation may be related to the site of electrode implantation.
the neuropsychological test performance of patients with PD who underwent thalamic electrode implantation did not deteriorate after surgery.
the mean changes in performance on a battery of neuropsychological tests were minimal and that the individual changes in performance were generally in the direction of improvement.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cognitive effects of thalamic stimulating electrodes in PD patients.
the study of the cognitive and emotional consequences of the deep brain stimulation in the VIM thalamic nucleus.
the cognitive safety and efficacy of thalamic deep brain stimulation (DBS) for the treatment of Parkinson's disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
thalamic stimulation is not a safe and efficacious treatment for the cognitive deficits associated with PD.
the cognitive safety of chronic thalatic stimulation for the treatment of tremor-dominan PD is not yet established.
chronic unilateral thalamic stimulation for PD is not associated with significant cognitive changes, but that the cognitive safety of this procedure has not been adequately established.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
chronic thalamic stimulating electrodes are safe for use in PD and may be a reasonable alternative to surgical lesioning procedures.
the cognitive effects of chronic thalomic stimulation in PD are not as severe as those of thalamic lesion.
chronic stimulation of the ventralis intermediate nucleus (VIM) of the thalamus does not produce cognitive impairment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the thalamus plays a critical role in cognitive function.
the cognitive safety of chronic thalomic stimulation in the treatment of refratory PD is supported.

chronic thalamic stimulating electrodes can be placed in patients with Parkinson's disease with minimal risk of cognitive morbidity, and the potential benefits of thalamic deep brain stimulation for patients with Parkinson's who are refractory to medical therapy are likely to outweigh the risks of cognitive side effects.
